Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported in these early weeks of motherhood. Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—better known as the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s just a quick way to see how your emotional health is doing and to make sure you’re getting any extra care you might need. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger. We’ll go through ten short questions about the past seven days; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. Ready to begin?

First question: In the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

I have—this week I still smiled at my morning coffee and even put on a podcast I like while folding the baby’s laundry. It’s not the same bubbly excitement I had before, but the little sparks are definitely still there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—my partner made a goofy face while changing a diaper blow-out the other night and I burst out giggling. It doesn’t feel forced or anything; the humor’s still coming naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do—like tomorrow I’m planning to meet my best friend for a short walk with the stroller, and I’m honestly looking forward to it. It’s not this huge thrill, but it’s a nice, steady feeling of “oh, that’ll be fun.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if the baby spits up right after I’ve changed him, I might think “maybe I jostled him too much,” but I shrug it off pretty fast. I don’t sit there beating myself up—babies spit up, it’s just what they do.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little, I guess. Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds normal or if the room temperature is okay, even when everything looks fine. It’s not constant—just quick flashes of worry that pass once I check on him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like that. I haven’t had any of those “heart racing, can’t catch my breath” moments—at least not this week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like yesterday when the baby wouldn’t settle and the dishes were piled up, I felt a bit overwhelmed for a minute. I took a breath, put him in the wrap, and got through it, but it can feel like a juggling act.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, that hasn’t happened. Once I finally lie down, I drift off pretty easily—exhaustion helps, I think. My main sleep trouble is just the baby’s night feeds, not my mind racing or feeling upset.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I’ve had a couple of teary moments when I’m extra tired, but overall I’ve felt okay—just normal new-mom ups and downs, nothing heavy or gloomy hanging around.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried at all this week. A few times my eyes stung from tiredness, but no actual tears—nothing felt that overwhelming.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind—not once.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS-10 (informal)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Fleeting, situational worry about infant well-being (Q4)  
- Occasional “getting on top of me” when multiple demands collide (Q6)

Symptoms denied  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, hopelessness  
- Loss of pleasure / inability to laugh or look forward to activities  
- Excessive or persistent guilt / self-blame  
- Panic-type episodes  
- Mood-related insomnia (sleep disruption limited to infant feeding schedule)  
- Self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Transient, manageable stress reactions without pervasive affective symptoms; no evidence of major depressive or anxiety episode at this time.

Risk factors present  
- First-time parenting stressors  
- Fatigue / role overload

Risk factors absent  
- Core neuro-vegetative or cognitive symptoms of depression  
- Safety concerns (nil self-harm)

Screening impression  
Low likelihood for current postpartum depression or anxiety disorder. Continue routine surveillance, psycho-education, and encourage support use; re-screen if clinical picture changes.
